by: Claude Code (opus), titles and abstracts only

question.population: Adults, healthy or with risk factors (reviews limited to one illness count as partly)
question.intervention: Blueberries: whole, juice or freeze-dried whole-blueberry powder

decisions.reason: Covers blood pressure in RCTs, but only in patients with cardiometabolic disease, and blueberry is pooled together with cranberry rather than clearly on its own.
Meta-analysis of blueberry intake in human studies that reports systolic and diastolic blood pressure among the metabolic syndrome outcomes.
RCTs of blueberry as fruit, juice or powder (plus some extracts) versus placebo, with blood pressure pooled as an outcome.
Meta-analysis of RCTs comparing blueberry supplementation with placebo on systolic and diastolic blood pressure.

question.population: Adults, healthy or with risk factors (reviews limited to one illness count as partly)
question.intervention: Blueberries: whole, juice or freeze-dried whole-blueberry powder

decisions.reason: Pooled human studies of blueberry intake and reported triglycerides, total, LDL and HDL cholesterol; the population was not limited to one illness.
Placebo-controlled trials with lipid outcomes, but blueberry extract was pooled with fruit, juice and powder, and no separate whole-food analysis is reported.
Controlled trials of blueberry, including powder and freeze-dried forms, versus control in adults, with triglycerides and other lipid outcomes pooled.

question.population: Adults, healthy or with risk factors (reviews limited to one illness count as partly)
question.intervention: Blueberries: whole, juice or freeze-dried whole-blueberry powder
question.comparison: Placebo powder or drink, or no blueberries
question.outcome: Blood vessel function (flow-mediated dilation) or arterial stiffness

decisions.reason: Meta-analysis of RCTs of blueberry consumption versus control in healthy adults that pooled flow-mediated dilation.
Meta-analysis of blueberry interventions in adults that pooled flow-mediated dilation as a measure of endothelial function.
Systematic review of human trials of blueberries and their bioactives in healthy and at-risk adults that covers vascular function markers.

question.population: Children or adults, often older adults
question.intervention: Blueberries: whole, juice or freeze-dried whole-blueberry powder

decisions.reason: Meta-analysis of RCTs of blueberry consumption in healthy people, with pooled cognitive (executive function) and mood outcomes.
Pooled RCTs of blueberry intake and memory, but only in older adults with prior cognitive decline, a narrower population.
Meta-analysis of randomised trials of blueberry intake on cognitive performance and mood in human studies.
Systematic review of RCTs of whole, freeze-dried and concentrate blueberry in children and adults, covering cognition and mood.
Systematic review of blueberry trials in children, older adults and people with MCI, with memory and executive function outcomes.
A comment on errors in an earlier review, not a systematic review itself.
An author reply to comments on an earlier review, not a systematic review itself.

question.population: Adults, healthy or with risk factors (reviews limited to one illness count as partly)
question.intervention: Blueberries: whole, juice or freeze-dried whole-blueberry powder
question.outcome: Blood sugar, HbA1c or insulin sensitivity

decisions.reason: Covers whole blueberry in obesity/diabetes, but pools bilberry and animal studies; glucose effects are reported mainly in rodents, not humans.
Meta-analysis of human blueberry studies reporting pooled HbA1c, glucose, HOMA-IR and insulin in adults with metabolic syndrome risk factors.
Meta-analysis of RCTs of blueberry (powder, fruit, juice, plus some extract) versus placebo, pooling glycemic markers in adults with metabolic risk.
Pools blueberry with cranberry for glucose, HbA1c and insulin resistance; the abstract does not report a blueberry-only analysis.
Combines blueberry and cranberry, including extracts, and is limited to adults with type 2 diabetes; the outcome is glycemic control.
Reviews whole blueberry intake, but outcomes are obesity and glycaemic markers (mostly in animals), not new type 2 diabetes.
Trials of blueberry or cranberry in people with or without diabetes; outcomes are glucose markers, not new type 2 diabetes.
Trials in adults who already have type 2 diabetes, looking at glycaemic control rather than new diabetes.
Meta-analysis of prospective cohorts on type 2 diabetes risk that analyses blueberries as a separate fruit subtype.
Meta-analysis of prospective cohorts that pools risk of type 2 diabetes for high versus low blueberry intake.
Pooled three cohorts of adults free of chronic disease and reports new type 2 diabetes per extra servings of blueberries.

question.intervention: Blueberries or related berries (bilberry, cranberry), as food, juice or whole-fruit powder
question.outcome: Muscle soreness, muscle damage, recovery or exercise performance

decisions.reason: Looks at blueberries and cognition and mood, not muscle soreness, recovery or exercise performance.
Looks at blueberries and cognitive performance in children and older adults, not exercise or muscle outcomes.
A comment on a review of blueberries and cognition, not a systematic review of exercise or muscle outcomes.
An author reply about a review of blueberries and cognition, not a review of exercise or muscle outcomes.
Reviews blueberry, cranberry and bilberry products against a control in healthy people, measuring exercise performance and recovery.
Covers many berries and mostly blackcurrant, with only a few blueberry studies (one in humans) and animal studies mixed in.
Looks at berry anthocyanins and cognition, vascular function and heart-health markers, not exercise or muscle outcomes.
